passages.original: inspectum volnus absterso cruore; omnia salubria esse; confidere prope diem ipsum eos visuros; interim Ser. Tullio iubere populum dicto audientem esse; eum iura redditurum obiturumque alia regis munia esse. Servius cum trabea et lictoribus prodit ac sede regia sedens alia decernit, de aliis consulturum se regem esse simulat. itaque per aliquot dies, cum iam exspirasset Tarquinius, celata morte per speciem alienae fungendae vicis suas opes firmavit.
passages.english: The wound had been examined after the blood was wiped away; everything was sound; she was confident that they would see him himself within a few days; meanwhile he ordered the people to be obedient to Servius Tullius; he would administer justice and perform the other duties of the king. Servius comes forth in the *trabea* [the striped robe of state] and with lictors, and sitting on the royal seat he decides some matters, and on others pretends that he will consult the king. So for several days, though Tarquinius had already expired, with his death concealed, under the appearance of discharging another's office he strengthened his own power.

passages.original: a quo facessere iussa ex tanto tumultu, cum se domum reciperet pervenissetque ad summum Cyprium vicum, ubi Dianium nuper fuit, flectenti carpentum dextra in Urbium clivum ut in collem Esquiliarum eveheretur, restitit pavidus atque inhibuit frenos is qui iumenta agebat, iacentemque dominae Servium trucidatum ostendit. foedum inhumanumque inde traditur scelus, monumentoque locus est—Sceleratum vicum vocant—quo amens agitantibus furiis sororis ac viri, Tullia per patris corpus carpentum egisse fertur, partemque sanguinis ac caedis paternae cruento vehiculo, contaminata ipsa respersaque, tulisse ad penates suos virique sui, quibus iratis malo regni principio similes propediem exitus sequerentur.
passages.english: Ordered by him to withdraw from so great a tumult, as she was returning home and had reached the top of the Cyprian Street, where the shrine of Diana stood until recently, as she was turning her carriage to the right onto the Urbian Slope to be carried up to the Esquiline hill, the man who was driving the animals stopped in terror and pulled in the reins, and pointed out to his mistress Servius lying slaughtered. A foul and inhuman crime is reported to have followed, and the place serves as a memorial (they call it the Street of Crime), where Tullia, out of her mind, driven by the avenging spirits of her sister and her husband, is said to have driven her carriage over her father's body, and, herself defiled and spattered, to have carried part of her father's blood and slaughter on the bloody vehicle to her own household gods and her husband's; and through their anger, an ending like the evil beginning of the reign would soon follow.
passages.notes: "furiis sororis ac viri": the Furies of her murdered sister and first husband.
